1.pericope_label: O Israel, return unto the Lord thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity. Take with you words, and turn to the Lord: say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips.

schools.summary: Ellicott finds tenderness and inextinguishable love in the pronoun of the opening address, quotes the rabbinic saying that repentance presses right up to the eternal throne, and renders the last clause accept of good, and we will render as calves our lips, so that the words of true repentance become the offering in place of animals.

Gill insists on a return quite up to God's seat rather than halfway, grounds the appeal on his being still their God by choice and covenant and redemption, and will not have mere words without the heart but words of confession. Calvin answers the objection that he had already denied any remedy remained, distinguishing the whole body of the people from the few still faithful, and uses the verse to attack a conception of repentance made up of fasts and muttered prayers and vowed pilgrimages.

Clarke lays out the design of the whole chapter, from the exhortation and its form of prayer through the promises drawn from the refreshing dews to the closing restriction of them to those who bring forth fruits of righteousness; on taking words he argues that a man may be sure he prays rightly when he uses words God himself has put in his mouth, and numbers the steps the verse prescribes. Wesley states the outcome plainly, that this qualifies them to give sacrifices more pleasing to God than calves or oxen.

Henry draws two lessons from the invitation: that sin is a fall, so those who have fallen by it must get up again by repentance, and that conversion must be preached to those inside the church as well as to the heathen, since being Israel makes the revolt more heinous and the return more necessary.

debates.question: How can a call to repent stand after the previous chapter's threat of final destruction?

positions.position: The threat had the whole body of the people in view, while this address turns to the few who remained faithful; without that distinction a reader is perplexed in many parts of scripture.
The evils, positively predicted as they are, might yet have been prevented on repentance.

debates.question: What is offered in place of calves?

positions.position: The words of true repentance themselves, rendered as calves, that is as the sacrificial offering.
Sacrifices more pleasing to God than calves or oxen, which the pardon qualifies and encourages them to give.
Words that come from the heart and express its true sense, by which sin is acknowledged and forgiveness asked.

outliers.claim: Turns the command to take words into a doctrine of prayer: a man may be assured he prays rightly when he uses the words God himself put in his mouth, which is what gives the Lord's Prayer a potency beyond any human composition, and probably why the reformers set it so often in the public liturgy.

Uses the verse against a whole conception of repentance, since men bring forward mere trifles when they speak of it, imagining that fasts and muttered prayers and vowed pilgrimages will pacify God, whereas the prophet sets out true repentance by its fruits.

themes: O Israel, return unto the Lord thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity.
Take with you words, and turn to the Lord: say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips.

3.pericope_label: Asshur shall not save us; we will not ride upon horses: neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, Ye are our gods: for in thee the fatherless findeth mercy. I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him.

schools.summary: Ellicott counts the three crying sins the verse renounces -- expecting salvation from one great power, depending on another famed for war-horses, and giving divine names to wrought images -- and glosses the closing clause as God's paternal love for the orphan, peculiarly applicable to a people cast on a cold and fatherless world; of the reply he says only that if the foregoing is the offering of penitent lips, it is full of superlative grace.

Gill matches the promise to heal against the petition that iniquity be taken away, and works the metaphor out, sins being diseases and backslidings relapses with one physician who heals both. Calvin makes the future verbs carry an indirect confession of past sin, and explains why the assurance of pardon had to be repeated, since when we embrace a promise of free pardon the flesh at once leads us to distrust.

Clarke numbers the parts of the answer as he had numbered the steps of the prayer, and takes the free love in a princely sense, a love that is beneficial and not merely affectionate, filling its objects with delight rather than only feeling it. Wesley widens the fatherless to all who are destitute of strength in themselves and of help from others, and takes the mercy named as both the fountain and the streams.

Henry states the principle behind the correspondence of prayer and promise, that if we speak to God in good prayers he will speak to us in good promises, and lays the turning away of the anger as the ground of every other favour, adding that God is not implacable in his anger, which shall be turned away from those who turn from their iniquity.

debates.question: Why is the assurance of pardon repeated?

positions.position: Because nothing is harder than keeping men dependent on the one God: embracing a promise of free pardon, the flesh at once leads us to distrust and we are harassed by the thought that we cannot dare promise ourselves a propitious God.
Because the turning away of the anger is the ground of all the other favours promised, and opens a door for every good to flow.

debates.question: What does loving them freely mean?

positions.position: In a princely and liberal manner: a beneficial love, not merely an affectionate one, which fills its objects with delight.
The majestic reply of superlative grace to the offering of penitent lips.
The healing of relapses by a fresh application of the physician's blood, which takes away sin and restores peace.

outliers.claim: Reads the future verbs of the renunciation as carrying an indirect confession, so that in promising not to trust foreign powers or images again the speakers admit they had already roused God's vengeance in exactly those ways.

Widens the fatherless past orphans to all who are destitute of strength in themselves and of help from others, and who, sensible of that helplessness, look for it from the one who has power and mercy and wisdom to help.

themes: Asshur shall not save us; we will not ride upon horses: neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, Ye are our gods: for in thee the fatherless findeth mercy.
I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him.

5.pericope_label: I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon. His branches shall spread, and his beauty shall be as the olive tree, and his smell as Lebanon. They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine: the scent thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon.

schools.summary: Ellicott alters the syntax of the shadow clause, holding it more in accordance with the Hebrew idiom that the dwellers under its shadow shall once more cause the corn to grow, corrects the last word from scent to renown, and observes that although the promises take their form from the external signs of national prosperity, corn and wine are throughout the scriptures the great symbols of spiritual refreshment.

Gill reads the dew as a promise of the latter-day conversion, takes the spreading branches for the propagation of the church in the first times of the gospel and again at the end, and canvasses three candidates for the shadow before preferring the Lord's own. Calvin makes the promise the other half of a lesson he had taught throughout, that the people would be miserable until they turned, and settles the disputed verb as meaning to be refreshed rather than to return.

Clarke borrows a bishop's observations on the climate, where dews preserve life as well as refresh, and explains the exactness of the corn image, whose side leaves fall back withered as the stalk pushes through, so that a stranger could see no hope of harvest. Wesley works the images separately, the olive keeping green through winter so that the true Israel flourishes in fruit and not in fruitless beauty even in winters of affliction.

positions.position: The Lord's own, to whom Israel was called to return; not the mountain's, nor the church's, though both were proposed.
The question is beside the point: the verb means to be refreshed, so what matters is that Israel's shadow will be vivifying to those who lie under it.
The idiom is better rendered so that the dwellers under its shadow shall once more cause the corn to grow.

debates.question: What do the promises of growth chiefly signify?

positions.position: The latter-day conversion, when churches shall be set up everywhere and the fulness of the Gentiles brought in.
The refreshing comforts of the gospel, figured by the dews that preserve life in a hot country.
Spiritual refreshment: the form is drawn from signs of national prosperity, but corn and wine are the scriptures' great symbols of it.
Fruit rather than fruitless beauty, borne even in winters of affliction.

outliers.claim: Explains why the comparison to corn is more exact than it appears: once the young plant is above ground its side leaves turn back to make way for the stalk and fall towards the earth with a withered look, so that a stranger seeing the field then could entertain no hope of a harvest.

Makes the promise the second half of a lesson he had pressed throughout the book: the people had imagined their adversities happened by chance, and had to be taught that they would be miserable until they turned and unhappy in all their affairs until they obtained pardon.

themes: I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon.
His branches shall spread, and his beauty shall be as the olive tree, and his smell as Lebanon.
They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine: the scent thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon.

8.pericope_label: Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols? I have heard him, and observed him: I am like a green fir tree. From me is thy fruit found.

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers a slightly different reading indicated by the Greek, giving as for Ephraim, what has he to do with idols, notes that the Hebrew for thy fruit plays on the name Ephraim as it had earlier in the book, and takes the evergreen tree as God's own speech, that he is to Ephraim a tree of life and protection from whom the fruit is found.

Gill denies that the speaker can be the Ephraim of the prophet's own day, who was given up as glued to his idols, and redefines the idols renounced as those of the heart, the unbelief and rejection of the Messiah and the traditions preferred to the written word. Calvin hears a confession rather than a resolution, and takes shame at oneself joined to a detestation of the former life as the testimony of true repentance.

Clarke would attach the evergreen tree to what precedes and make the whole a speech of God, so that the sense is I have heard him and seen him as a flourishing tree; on the last clause he holds that all goodness springs from a principle of grace planted in the soul, since the soul of even the most pious cannot bear fruit without a continual influence from above. Wesley keeps the image on the human side, a weary traveller finding rest under a thick tree.

Henry reports both a reading in which God argues with Ephraim about what he and idols have to do with each other and one in which God promises to bring him to say it, prefers the second, and draws from it that God's promises to us are a better security for mortifying sin than our promises to God.

debates.question: Is the renunciation a promise, an argument, or a confession?

positions.position: A promise that God will bring Ephraim to say it and keep him to it, which is better security than any promise of ours.
A confession, in which the people deplore their blindness and folly and detest their whole former life.
A question about Ephraim rather than by him, on the reading indicated by the Greek.

debates.question: Who speaks the words about the evergreen tree?

positions.position: God, the clause belonging with what precedes: I have heard him and seen him as a flourishing tree.
The image is of the believer's shelter, as a weary traveller finds rest and safety under a thick tree.
Not graven images, which have not tempted the Jewish people since the captivity, but the idols of the heart: unbelief, rejection of the Messiah, and the traditions preferred to the written word.
The superstitions the ten tribes had alienated themselves to, renounced for the future.

outliers.claim: Argues that as the earth cannot bear fruit without dew and rain and sun, so the soul of even the most pious cannot bear fruit without a continual influence from the Most High.

Redefines the idols of the promise for a later age, since graven images have not tempted the Jewish people since the captivity, so that what will be renounced at their conversion is unbelief, the rejection of the Messiah, and the traditions of the elders.

themes: Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols? I have heard him, and observed him: I am like a green fir tree. From me is thy fruit found.

9.pericope_label: Who is wise, and he shall understand these things? prudent, and he shall know them? for the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them: but the transgressors shall fall therein.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the closing question as the prophet handing his words over to all students of the ways of God, and observes that in the later Hebrew literature wisdom and wise men take the place that prophecy and prophets had held, wisdom being what interprets both the word and its fulfilment.

Calvin hears amazement in the question at how few yielded to be taught, explains the verse as the sealing of a book whose teaching had to be reduced into brief heads at the end, describes the pride it rebukes in the terms of his own century as well as the prophet's, and turns the word round at the close, since true wisdom is to obey God and the beginning of wisdom is the fear of him.

Clarke answers what the things are from the chapter itself, makes understanding conditional on endeavouring and laying the heart to them, and argues that all God's conduct in justice and mercy is right because he is too wise to err and too good to be unkind; he warns that men once good may fall in the way of righteousness itself. Wesley divides the ways into those we walk towards God and those in which he walks towards us, and calls both righteous and equal.

Henry makes the last clause the most frightening thing in the chapter: the same stone is a foundation to some and a stumbling-block to others, what was ordained to life becomes death through abuse of it as the same sun softens wax and hardens clay, and the most dangerous falls of all are those of men who fall in the ways of God.

debates.question: Why does the chapter end with a question?

positions.position: Because the prophet hands his words over to all students of God's ways, the exhortation to wisdom taking the form of a question.
Because he was amazed at the fewness of those who yielded themselves to be taught, and challenges men who thought themselves acute to acknowledge that he was sent.

debates.question: What are these things that the wise shall understand?

positions.position: The backslidings and punishment of Israel, the mercy of the promised restoration, the work of sin in the heart and the work of grace in the soul.
What the prophet has delivered throughout, both the ways we are to walk towards God and the ways he walks towards us.
Whatever a man sets himself to understand and know; those who do so profit by the truths delivered.

debates.question: How do transgressors fall in the very ways of God?

positions.position: By stumbling at the commands and still more at the judgments, casting off the one and hoping vainly to shift the other.
By continuing to use the ordinances and keep company with God's people while ceasing to depend on God for light and life and power.
By abusing what was ordained to life until it becomes death, as the same sun softens wax and hardens clay; these are the most dangerous falls of all.

outliers.claim: Explains the shape of the book from this verse: prophets reduced into brief heads at the end what they had taught at length, since it is absurd to suppose a man who held the office so long said only what could be gone through in three hours.

Describes the scoffers of his own century in the same breath as the prophet's, men who count it simplicity to believe anything scripture contains, ask what faith is but foolish credulity, and taunt that believing means giving up all judgment and being driven like mute cattle.

themes: Who is wise, and he shall understand these things? prudent, and he shall know them? for the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them: but the transgressors shall fall therein.
